Recognize when records describe variables occurring together.

Distinguish the partly hidden world, observed data, and a model of how the world may work.
Distinguish a pattern supported by data from a causal assumption.
Use node, arrow, path, and DAG as names for visible causal-model assumptions.
Recognize that a cause can change a probability without determining every individual outcome.

resources.text: A clinic records each patient's resting heart rate. Could resting heart rate be a variable?
A dashboard records the number of alerts each hour. Is the alert count a variable?
Ask whether the item could have a different value for another record or time.
A variable is a recorded feature that can take different values across cases or times.
Yes. Different patients or hours can have different values, so this is a variable.
The value is not fixed by the story; it can vary across records, which is what makes it a variable.
Records show that people who exercise more often also report lower resting heart rates. What can we say about this relationship based on these observations?
A product log shows that users who save drafts more often also finish more documents. Does the log show an observed association?
Look for two recorded variables that occur together or vary together.
An association is a pattern in records: values of two variables occur or vary together.
Yes. The records describe how two variables vary together; that is an observed association.
The question asks only whether the recorded pattern co-occurs, not whether it has already established a cause.
We observe that ice-cream sales and sunglasses sales rise together. Does this observation alone establish that increased ice-cream sales cause an increase in sunglasses sales?
A synthetic campus log records umbrella carrying and wet pavement. Would giving everyone an umbrella change how often the pavement is wet? Investigate before making that claim.
Ask whether another cause or another causal direction could fit the same observed pattern.
A pattern in records can be associated without telling us the causal direction or mechanism.
Correct choice: the observed pattern alone does not establish a causal direction. This records one classification, not mastery of causal reasoning.
Treating co-occurrence as a causal direction skips the assumptions needed to distinguish causal explanations.

Mission: would making everyone carry an umbrella change how often the pavement is wet? Inspect the campus records, propose a model and prediction, reveal the teaching model's result, then revise your explanation.

Each record is one person's arrival at campus. Pavement wetness describes the pavement at that arrival. These are 240 arrival records, not 240 different days. The records show umbrella carrying and wet pavement together, but do not say why.

Arrows are proposed causes, not facts established by the records. Compare umbrella carrying causing wet pavement, the reverse direction, or rain as a common cause. More than one model can fit these observations.
Imagine the same 240 arrivals, with umbrella carrying deliberately set to yes for everyone. What do you predict would happen to how often the pavement is wet?

Keep all 240 arrival records and the same background conditions. Set umbrella carrying to yes for everyone, including the 144 arrivals originally without an umbrella. This changes carrying; it does not select only the original umbrella carriers. Reveal the prewritten result for this teaching model; it is not calculated from your proposed arrows.

All 240 arrival records remain: 96 wet and 144 dry, so 40% are wet, unchanged from before. Filtering the original records to umbrella carriers would instead retain only 96 records, all wet (100%). Selecting existing carriers and making everyone carry an umbrella are different comparisons. This is the supplied teaching model's result, not a real-world experiment.

Compare your prediction with the unchanged wet-pavement proportion. This one test does not uniquely identify a graph. For the final model-building exercise, use these supplied assumptions: rain causes umbrella carrying and pavement wetness, with no other direct arrows among these three variables. Revise your graph and separate what came from the test from what was supplied.

Making everyone carry an umbrella left pavement wetness unchanged in this teaching model. Filtering the original umbrella carriers would have produced a different proportion. The final graph check asks you to represent the supplied assumptions: rain causes umbrella carrying and wet pavement, with no other direct arrows among these variables. The test alone did not identify a unique graph. Your prediction and reflection are recorded, not scored as correct reasoning.
A clinician asks whether a patient's recovery would change if they were given a different drug dose. Is this a causal question?
A product manager asks: what would happen to retention if the team changed the onboarding flow? Is this a treatment-and-outcome question?
Identify what is deliberately changed and which result is being asked about.
Treatment-and-outcome reasoning asks about changing one variable and the resulting outcome.
Yes. The question explicitly asks about changing a treatment and the outcome that follows.
The key feature is the proposed change to a treatment and its outcome, not merely a pattern already recorded.
A clinic records its patients' existing sleep durations without assigning a sleep schedule. Is the clinic observing sleep or intervening on it?
A team compares users who already chose focus mode with those who did not. Is this observation or an intervention on focus mode?
Ask who deliberately set the value, rather than merely recording an existing value.
Observation records existing values. An intervention deliberately sets or changes a value.
Correct. No one assigned the value, so the evidence is observational rather than interventional.
Recording or comparing existing choices is not the same as deliberately setting the value.
A researcher draws a diagram explaining how a hidden disease process might generate observed data records. Is the diagram data or a model?
An engineer writes an explanation of how a hidden service dependency may produce outage logs. Is the explanation data or a model?
Separate the records we can see from an explanation of the partly hidden system.
Data are observed records; a model is an explanation of how the partly hidden world may work.
Correct. The drawing is an explanatory model, not the data themselves.
An explanation of hidden processes is a model; the observed logs or records are the data.
A dataset shows that people carrying umbrellas are often near wet streets. Is the claim that rain causes both an observation directly supported by these records, or an additional causal assumption?
A log shows that people who open help pages submit more bug reports. Is the claim that confusion causes both behaviors an observation or an assumption?
Ask whether the statement reports a recorded pattern or adds a causal mechanism to explain it.
Data can support an observed pattern. A causal direction or mechanism is an additional assumption that should be stated.
Correct. The causal explanation goes beyond the observed pattern, so it is an assumption.
The records may support co-occurrence, but they do not directly record the proposed causal explanation.
In a proposed causal diagram, what does an arrow from sleep to concentration represent?
In a diagram of focus mode and typing errors, what does a connected route through arrows represent: a path or a node?
Recall that nodes name variables, arrows name proposed directions, and connected routes are paths.
A node represents a variable, an arrow a proposed direction, and a path a connected route through arrows in a DAG.
Correct. The named graphical feature makes an assumption visible; it is not an observed numeric value.
Keep the graph terms separate: nodes are variables, arrows are directions, and paths are connected routes.
Suppose a treatment raises the chance of recovery, but some treated patients still do not recover. Is the effect probabilistic or deterministic?
Suppose providing a tutorial increases the chance that people keep using a digital service, but some people still stop using it. Is the effect probabilistic or deterministic?
Ask whether the cause changes what is likely, or guarantees the same outcome for every individual.
A causal effect can change an outcome probability without determining every individual result.
Correct. The cause changes a probability, not a guaranteed outcome for every individual.
A changed chance is not a guarantee. Individual outcomes can still differ under a probabilistic effect.
A research team records voluntary sleep, concentration, and recovery, then draws a DAG to explain the pattern. Which conclusion is justified without adding an assumption?
Separate the recorded association from the causal model and from what would happen if sleep were deliberately assigned.
The records establish an association. The DAG is a model with explicit causal assumptions, and an intervention would require deliberately setting sleep rather than only observing it.
Correct choice on this association-versus-causation check. The records do not establish the proposed intervention effect. This single decision does not assess all nine M0 concepts.
That conclusion treats an observed pattern and a model drawing as if they already proved an intervention effect. Those are different kinds of information.

Represent the supplied simulator assumptions, not a graph claimed to be uniquely discovered: rain causes both umbrella carrying and pavement wetness, with no other direct arrows among these three variables.
Your graph matches the supplied simulator assumptions. This is a model-representation check, not proof that the data identified a unique graph. Your prediction and reflection remain unscored.

This graph does not yet represent the supplied simulator assumptions. For this exercise, include rain causing umbrella carrying and wet pavement, with no other direct arrows. Other graphs may fit the observed pattern; this check is not causal discovery.
A clinic records resting heart rates of 64, 72 and 80 beats per minute. What stays the same across the three records, and what changes?
Synthetic teaching records; no real patient measurements. Expert content review pending.
Resting heart rate is the feature recorded for each person. Its name tells us what to look for in every row.
For one record, the value is 72 beats per minute. The number is a value of heart rate, not a different variable.
Other records can have different values of the same feature. A variable need not change in every row; it needs to be capable of taking different values.
A variable is a feature that can take different values. A value is a particular instance of that feature, such as one recorded heart rate.
Do not confuse the variable's name with one person's value. A constant value in a small sample does not, by itself, make a feature incapable of varying.
Ask: what feature are we recording, and what value does it have in this case?
Records show that people reporting more weekly exercise also tend to have lower resting heart rates. What does the recorded pattern describe?
Synthetic teaching example; not an empirical exercise study. Expert content review pending.
The records contain reported exercise and resting heart rate. Each person contributes values for both features.
In this dataset, higher exercise values occur alongside lower heart-rate values. Variables can be associated while moving in opposite directions.
Say which values tend to occur together across the records. One isolated heart-rate reading is not itself a pattern between the two variables.
An observed association is a pattern in how variables occur together or vary together in the records.
Association does not require both variables to increase. One can tend to decrease as the other increases.
First describe the recorded relationship between the variables in plain language.
A city records that ice-cream sales and sunglasses sales rise together. Would stopping ice-cream sales change sunglasses sales?
Synthetic city example; proposed explanations are hypotheses. Expert content review pending.
The records describe sales rising together. That is a statement about the observed pattern, not the result of an action on either shop.
Warm, sunny days could influence both purchases. This is a possible shared explanation; proposing it does not establish that it is the true explanation.
Stopping ice-cream sales changes one part of the situation. The recorded association alone does not tell us whether sunglasses sales would change.
This partial hypothetical graph shows a possible shared cause. It does not settle the effect of changing either kind of sale.
Association describes how variables vary together. An observed association alone does not establish which variable causes the other or what an intervention would do.
Do not turn co-occurrence into a causal conclusion. A plausible common cause is also not proof that there is no effect between the variables.
Keep the observed pattern, a proposed explanation and the effect of an action separate.
A question asks whether giving a different drug dose would change recovery. Which part is the proposed change, and which part is the result?
Synthetic question; no drug benefit or dosing recommendation is asserted. Expert content review pending.
The drug dose is the feature the question proposes changing. In causal reasoning, the word treatment names the intervention of interest.
Recovery is the result the question asks about. Naming it tells us what consequence of the change we want to understand.
What would happen to recovery if the dose were changed? Recognising this question type does not answer whether the change would help.
A treatment-and-outcome question asks what happens to an outcome when a treatment is changed. Treatment can also mean a non-medical intervention, such as a changed service process.
Naming a treatment and outcome is not evidence that the treatment has a beneficial effect.
Complete the sentence: if we changed this treatment, what would happen to this outcome?
A clinic records how long patients already sleep. Has recording those values changed anyone's sleep duration?
Synthetic teaching example; no sleep intervention or health effect is asserted. Expert content review pending.
The clinic reads durations that already occurred. The act described in this example is recording existing values.
A different example would deliberately assign a sleep schedule. That would change how the value was set rather than simply read it.
Sorting people by their existing durations is still observation. Ask whether someone deliberately set the value, not just whether two groups were compared.
Observation records existing values. An intervention deliberately sets or changes a variable, replacing how that value would otherwise be produced.
Selecting cases with a particular value is not the same action as setting that value.
Ask who, if anyone, assigned the value in the situation being described.
A researcher has measurements and a sketch of a hidden disease process. Are the measurements and the sketch the same kind of information?
Synthetic records and proposed explanation; not a verified disease mechanism. Expert content review pending.
The world is the system producing the observations. Its processes may be only partly visible to the researcher.
The recorded measurements are data. They show what was observed, rather than every hidden step that produced it.
The sketch is a proposed explanation of how the system might work. It represents the researcher's model rather than another measured record.
The world is the partly hidden system, data are its observed records, and a model is an explanation of how that system may work.
A well-drawn explanation does not become observed data merely because it looks precise.
Label each piece of information: system, observation or explanatory model.
A museum records that days with more donations also tend to have higher cafe sales. Does this pattern alone establish that visitor numbers cause both?
Hypothetical museum records and proposed explanation; not an empirical finding.
The records contain donations and cafe sales. Higher donations tend to occur on days with higher cafe sales: this is the observed pattern.
More visitors could lead to both more donations and more cafe sales. That is a proposed causal explanation, not a direct observation of what causes the pattern.

Write the two statements separately: donations and cafe sales are associated in the records; our proposed explanation assumes that visitor numbers influence both. The pattern alone does not establish that explanation.
Data can support an observed pattern. A causal direction or mechanism adds an assumption about how the pattern is produced.
A familiar or plausible explanation is still different from a direct observation of that explanation.
Use separate sentences for what the records show and what the causal explanation assumes.
In the umbrella investigation you proposed that rain influences both umbrella carrying and wet pavement. We can now give that picture a formal name: a directed acyclic graph, or DAG.
Synthetic proposed diagram; arrows are assumptions, not measured effects. Expert content review pending.
Rain, umbrella carrying and pavement wetness are variables. Each box is a node; a particular rainy arrival is a value or case, not another node.

Rain → umbrella carrying and Rain → pavement wetness represent the simulator's supplied causal assumptions. They are not effect sizes, and the observational table alone did not prove those directions.

Umbrella carrying ← Rain → pavement wetness is a path through a common cause. It is not a directed path from umbrellas to wet pavement. The graph is acyclic because following arrow directions never brings you back to the starting node.
The earlier intervention left wetness unchanged. The complete two-arrow diagram additionally uses the simulator's supplied assumptions; that one test did not uniquely identify this graph.
In a DAG, nodes represent variables, arrows represent proposed directions, and paths are connected routes through arrows.
Do not read an arrow as a recorded number or as proof that the proposed direction is true.
Name the graphical feature first: node, arrow or path. Then ask which assumption it represents.
Suppose giving Treatment T increases the chance of recovery, but some treated patients still do not recover. Can both statements be true?
Hypothetical treatment example; not a clinical finding or recommendation.
The example says that recovery is more likely with Treatment T than without it.
More likely does not mean certain. Some treated patients may still not recover.
A treatment can change the chance of recovery without guaranteeing recovery for every patient.
A cause can change an outcome's probability without determining every individual outcome.
One patient not recovering does not contradict a higher chance of recovery. This hypothetical example does not establish a real treatment benefit.
Separate a better chance from a guaranteed result.

The variable is the feature collected for every person. Zero, two and four are possible values of that feature.

Reconsider the distinction in this question. The variable is the feature collected for every person. Zero, two and four are possible values of that feature.

The deliberate assignment is the intervention. Random assignment does not guarantee a beneficial effect or an identical outcome for everyone.
Separate the recorded information, the proposed explanation and the deliberately assigned action.
The deliberate assignment is the intervention. Random assignment does not guarantee a beneficial effect or an identical outcome for everyone.
Reconsider the distinction in this question. The deliberate assignment is the intervention. Random assignment does not guarantee a beneficial effect or an identical outcome for everyone.

A proposed mechanism belongs to the model. It may concern an unmeasured part of the world, but proposing it does not make it observed data or establish that it is true.

At least three sessions | 20 | 74
Fewer than three sessions | 20 | 62
A claim about what causes attendance and scores is an additional causal assumption. Row counts, recorded means and recorded columns describe the data.
Separate the recorded information, the proposed explanation and the deliberately assigned action.
A claim about what causes attendance and scores is an additional causal assumption. Row counts, recorded means and recorded columns describe the data.
Reconsider the distinction in this question. A claim about what causes attendance and scores is an additional causal assumption. Row counts, recorded means and recorded columns describe the data.

Following both arrows gives a directed path through sessions attended. There is no arrow returning to Offer, and drawing the path does not estimate an effect size.

The stipulated chance increases by 0.20, or 20 percentage points. A probability of 0.60 still permits failures; these simulator rules are not a real-world effect estimate.
